# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-37 (Extended v236)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to summer Year 10, and 1784-1820 (Marseilles/Pharaon timeline). Key Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Champs-Élysées, Rue Saint-Honoré, Luxembourg Garden, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Temple, sewers (Sainte-Avoye, Louvre, Montmartre, belt, Amelot, Beautreillis), Marais, Blancs-Manteaux, Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, Rue de l'Écharpe, Rue Pavée, Rue des Trois-Pavillons, Saint-Paul church, Rue Beautreillis near Arsenal, Grand Sewer, Rue de l'Hôpital, Père-Lachaise cemetery, Rue Mondétour, Tuileries, Rue Saint-Jacques, Rue de la Jussienne, Rue Coq-Héron, Rue Bussy, Lyons, Grenoble. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Wilholt, Torton, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Gulhaven. Marseilles: La Canebière, Rue de Noailles, Allées de Meilhan, Rue du Grand Cours, Rue de l'Homme Armé, Medusa fountain, Palais de Justice, Accoules clock-tower, Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis, La Consigne, Frioul, Pilon, Porto-Ferrajo, Naples, Elba, Island of Elba, Point des Catalans, Ile Ratonneau, Rue de la Loge, Catalans, Madrid, Cape Pharo, Cape de Morgiou, Château d'If. **Timeline: 1814-1820 Marseilles; 1 March 1814 Dantès' arrest; spring Year 10 (1833) current time in English subplot.**

## English Subplot Summary (through Chapter 37, spring Year 10)

**Established solemn promises**: Semor swore to Isric Thornmere to rebuild fallen wall at Kelmere (summer Year 9). Elra gave Matho promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven; Pelia gave Fenelle promise to plant orchard above Salcombe (summer Year 7); Movie swore to Nerine promise to plant orchard above Wilholt (autumn Year 7); Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair chapel roof at Kelmere (winter Year 8); Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest; Kassa's husband swore to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe. Yera Haskick gave Lurald Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Quenford (winter Year 9). Eldest daughter of Lura Haskick kept promise made to Nerine Prydenridge: chapel roof repair at Kelmere completed by harvest (winter Year 9). Fewyn gave Havus Stenworth solemn promise to carry a sealed letter to Salcombe (winter Year 9). Luena gave husband of Yera Stenworth solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Haskick family (winter Year 9).

**Chapter 34-35 migrations**: Taric Corrley moved from Dungate to Kelmere with Kassa Stenson. Luena Stenenridge's only son moved from Ostcombe to Elmhaven. Pelde Stenworth married Sebin Brackick at Torton; couple lived in Torton thereafter. Fewyn Stenworth moved from Gulhaven to Yarlby with Havus. Pelia Lindmere moved to Yarlby with Rorald Lindmere. Havie Prydenridge found work in Staveford, moved there; Isric Thornmere followed her within the month. Youngest daughter of Fewyn Stenworth was apprenticed anew and became a herbalist. Youngest son of Nelan Brackick was apprenticed anew and became a weaver.

**Chapter 36-37 winter/spring scenes and rumors**: Frost silvered hedges; light went early; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; smoke lay flat over fields; wind carried salt and tar smell; road rutted and puddled after thaw. Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage. Multiple characters hummed childhood tunes while scrubbing steps (Rovus, Ismira, Isric, Yewyn, Movus). Ismira and Movus fell asleep in chairs before fire caught. Ismira laughed at story nobody else found funny. **RUMOR—Isric Thornmere told Havie Prydenridge old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar.** Movus Brackick bought ribbon at stall and regretted it; counted coins twice, came up penny short. Isric Thornmere won copper chalice from Gadrek Prydenridge at cards fairly. Jotho Thornmere mended torn sleeve. **Late one night Kassa Brackick confided to Davus that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood.** Baker's boy late; line at oven grew long. Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Movus mended torn sleeve by window, said little. Rorald and Fewyn Stenworth talked of weather, harvest, lame horse. Rorald read almanac aloud, mispronouncing saints. Yewyn Haskick complained of aching back. Dog barked at nothing then went quiet. Salt price repeatedly discussed; Gadrek laughed at story nobody else found funny; Rozek Stenenridge pressed jade mirror into Luvie Prydenridge's hands; Yewyn and Rozek sorted old letters by candlelight; Rorald Lindmere and others sorted letters; children chased hoop; Havus fell asleep in chair; Luvie remarked river was up again. **Ismira Stenson died that summer from festering wound; buried at Kelmere.** **A son born to Luvie Prydenridge and Semor Brackick, named Brevus Brackick; family lived in Ostcombe.** Rain threatened since morning but held off. Light went early. Yewyn Corrford complained of aching back as usual; mentioned salt price scandal. Yewyn Corrford hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step. Rovus Prydenridge told Wenelle he looked tired; Wenelle did not deny it. Brevus read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half the saints. Brevus spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight. Wenelle Lindmere bought ribbon at stall and regretted it. **Multiple characters asked: "Will it rain, do you think?"** (Gadrek to Nerine; Luena to Lurald; Luena to Brevus Brackick; Rovus to Wenelle). **The bone compass which Ismira Stenson had owned went to Matho Stenson.** **Kadan counted the coins twice and still came up a penny short.** **Yewyn walked the long way round to avoid the muddy square.** **Febin Prydenridge and Yewyn Corrford talked of nothing much—the weather, the harvest, a lame horse.** **Davus remarked salt price is a scandal; Elvie Brackick agreed.**

## Marseilles/Pharaon Subplot (1814-1820): Dantès' Arrest, Imprisonment, and Napoleonic Upheaval

**Edmond Dantès' arrival and engagement (1814)**: Young sailor Edmond Dantès jumped into skiff at La Canebière. Dantès ascended Allées de Meilhan, found father training nasturtiums and clematis. Reported Captain Leclere dead; would become captain with M. Morrel's aid. Captain at twenty, hundred louis pay, share in profits. Observed greedy glance in Caderousse's dark eyes.

**Fernand and Mercédès tragedy**: Fernand begged Mercédès to repeat refusal; ten years of marriage dreams ruined. Mercédès replied she never encouraged hope; always said she loved him as brother; heart belonged to another. **When Fernand asked final determination, Mercédès declared: if misfortune occur to Edmond, she would ascend Cape de Morgiou and cast herself headlong from it.** Later, Dantès and Mercédès clasped in each other's arms. Dantès saw Fernand's gloomy, pale, threatening countenance; Fernand placed hand on knife; Dantès extended cordial hand; Fernand remained mute and trembling.

**Danglars' denunciation and Caderousse's intervention**: Danglars feared being between drunkard and coward. Proposed to Fernand: write denunciation with left hand (handwriting unrecognizable). Wrote letter to king's attorney naming Edmond Dantès as Murat's agent carrying letters for usurper and Bonapartist committee. Caderousse, after reading letter, comprehended misery it must entail: "Yes, and that's all settled; only it will be an infamous shame." Stretched hand to reach letter; Danglars took it beyond reach, claimed jest, squeezed letter and threw into arbor corner. Earlier, Caderousse said: "Kill Dantès! who talks of killing Dantès? I won't have him killed. He's my friend, and this morning offered to share his money with me."

**1814 wedding and feast at La Réserve (1 March morning)**: M. Morrel had repeated promise that Dantès should succeed late Captain Leclere. Edmond placed arm of affianced bride within that of M. Morrel. Mercédès, lovely as Greek girls, with bright flashing jet eyes and ripe coral lips, moved with light, free step. At table centre, Mercédès said "Father," pointing to father on her right; on her left she placed Fernand, "him who has ever been as a brother to me," with soft, gentle smile. Her words inflicted direst torture on Fernand; his lips became ghastly pale. Dantès' old father carried glass of topaz-hued wine to lips. Dantès explained: "Thanks to M. Morrel's influence, all difficulties removed. Permission waived usual delay; at half-past two o'clock Mayor of Marseilles will be waiting at city hall. Tomorrow he starts for Paris; four days to go, four to return, one to discharge commission, back by first of March. On second he gives real marriage feast."

**Arrest and Villefort's interrogation (1 March, during feast)**: Danglars, observing Fernand's look, saw him stagger and fall convulsively against seat near open window. Indistinct sound on stairs, measured tread of soldiery, clanking of swords. Loud voice: "I demand admittance in the name of the law!" Magistrate wearing official scarf presented himself with four soldiers and corporal. Announced: "I am bearer of order of arrest." M. Morrel felt resistance useless. Old Dantès prayed and supplicated; Dantès surrendered. Long terrified silence followed. Old father and Mercédès remained apart absorbed in grief; at length rushed into each other's arms. Fernand appeared, poured glass of water with trembling hand, sat next to Mercédès, instinctively drew back chair. Villefort took packet from gendarme, disappeared. Dantès entered pale but calm, saluting judge with easy politeness. When asked political opinions, Dantès replied: "I never had any opinions. I am hardly nineteen... I love my father, I respect M. Morrel, and I adore Mercédès." **Regarding Captain Leclere's death and commission: "What I ought to have done, and what everyone would have done in my place... I sailed for Island of Elba, arrived next day; found difficulty obtaining access to grand-marshal; sent ring received from captain; was instantly admitted. He questioned me concerning Captain Leclere's death; gave me letter to carry to person in Paris. I undertook it because it was what my captain bade me do."** Villefort said: "This seems truth... Give up letter from Elba, pass word you will appear if required, go rejoin friends." **Villefort had destroyed the fatal letter—only proof against Dantès.**

**Villefort's remorse and decision to sacrifice Dantès (1 March evening)**: First pangs of unending torture seized Villefort's heart. Innocent victim Edmond appeared pale and threatening, leading Mercédès by hand, bringing remorse—slow and consuming agony. **Mercédès, hearing no news, came unobserved to inquire after him at Villefort's door.** Villefort pushed by her, closed door. But remorse not thus banished; like Virgil's wounded hero, he carried arrow in his wound. At salon, uttered sigh almost a sob, sank into chair. If sweet voice of Renée had pleaded for mercy, or fair Mercédès entered with plea, his cold trembling hands would have signed release; but no voice broke stillness. Door opened only by valet announcing travelling carriage. Villefort sprang from chair, hastily opened drawer, emptied gold into pocket, stood motionless hand pressed to head, muttered inarticulate sounds. **The hapless Dantès was doomed.**

**Villefort stands watching Noirtier's escape and travel to Lyons/Marseilles**: Villefort stood breathing, watching until father Noirtier disappeared at Rue Bussy. Then Villefort put black cravat and blue frock-coat at bottom of portmanteau, threw hat into dark closet, broke cane into small bits and flung in fire, put on travelling-cap, called valet, paid bill, sprang into carriage which was ready, learned at Lyons that Bonaparte had entered Grenoble, and reached Marseilles prey to hopes and fears of ambition and its first successes.

**Villefort's audience with King Louis XVIII and Noirtier's transformation**: Villefort arrived at Tuileries in dusty garb. King Louis XVIII sat before walnut table from Hartwell, carelessly listening to Blacas' warnings of Napoleon's danger. Villefort reported discovery of actual conspiracy—usurper arming three ships to land at Naples, Tuscany, or France coast; sailor arrested in Marseilles secretly visited Island of Elba and carried oral message from grand-marshal to Bonapartist in Paris preparing men's minds for return. King replied praise and declared royal gratitude will never forget service. Villefort stated: "Sire, the suddenness of this event must prove to your majesty that the issue is in the hands of Providence... Do not attribute to me more than I deserve." King later mentioned General Quesnel's death, wondering if result of murder rather than suicide; met unknown person at Rue Saint-Jacques. Police minister described suspect: fifty to fifty-two years old, dark, black eyes with shaggy eyebrows, thick moustache, blue frock-coat buttoned to chin, rosette of Legion of Honor. Villefort turned red and pale, leaned on armchair; but when learned unknown had escaped, breathed again. King detached cross of Legion of Honor and gave it to Villefort. **Noirtier—Villefort's father—cut off compromising whiskers, took colored neckerchief instead of black cravat, put on Villefort's dark brown coat cut away in front, tried narrow-brimmed hat, took up bamboo switch, walked with easy swagger, passed cool and collected by two or three ill-looking men at corner of street.**

**Imprisonment and Dantès' despair (1 March afternoon/evening onward)**: Through Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis to quay. Saw lights of La Consigne. Officer opened door; passage formed between soldier ranks. Boat drifted; four oarsmen impelled rapidly towards Pilon. Chain closing port lowered; in second they were in Frioul. Dantès saw light of Point des Catalans where Mercédès dwelt. Rose and perceived within hundred yards black and frowning Château d'If. Gendarme placed knee on chest: "Good! This is the way you keep your word as sailor!" Levelled carbine at Dantès. Dantès remained motionless, gnashing teeth, wringing hands with fury. Like man in dream; did not see ocean, terrible barrier against freedom. Followed guide into room almost underground, bare reeking walls, lamp on stool illumined apartment faintly. Jailer said: "Here is your chamber for tonight... Bread, water, and fresh straw; that is all a prisoner can wish for. Goodnight." Before Dantès could open mouth, jailer disappeared, taking lamp. Dantès alone in darkness and silence. Passed night standing without sleep. Scarcely tasted food; walked round cell like wild beast in cage. One thought tormented him: during journey he sat still, whereas he might dozen times have plunged into sea, thanks to swimming powers, gained shore, concealed himself, escaped to Spain or Italy, where Mercédès and father could have joined him. Would have been free and happy, whereas now confined in Château d'If, ignorant of father's and Mercédès' future; all because he trusted Villefort's promise. Thought was maddening. Next morning, jailer came again. Descended fifteen steps; door of dungeon opened; thrust in. Door closed; advanced with outstretched hands until touched wall; sat in corner until eyes became accustomed to darkness. Jailer was right; wanted but little of being utterly mad.

**Fernand's military service and Mercédès' devotion**: Fernand understood nothing except that Dantès was absent. What had become of him he cared not to inquire. Reflected partly on means of deceiving Mercédès as to cause of his absence, partly on plans of emigration and abduction, as from time to time he sat sad and motionless on summit of Cape Pharo, watching for apparition of young and handsome man, who was for him also messenger of vengeance. Fernand's mind was made up; he would shoot Dantès, and then kill himself. But Fernand was mistaken; a man of his disposition never kills himself, for he constantly hopes. During empire's last conscription, every man in France capable of bearing arms rushed to obey emperor's summons. Fernand departed with rest, bearing terrible thought that while away, his rival would perhaps return and marry Mercédès. Had Fernand really meant to kill himself, he would have done so when he parted from Mercédès. His devotion and compassion shown for her misfortunes produced effect they always produce on noble minds—Mercédès had always had sincere regard for Fernand, and this was now strengthened by gratitude.

**Aftermath and Napoleonic restoration (1815)**: **Mercédès left alone face to face with vast plain that had never seemed so barren, and sea that had never seemed so vast. Bathed in tears she wandered about Catalan village. Sometimes stood mute and motionless as statue, looking towards Marseilles, at other times gazing on sea, debating whether not better to cast herself into abyss of ocean, and thus end her woes. Not want of courage that prevented her putting this resolution into execution; but her religious feelings came to her aid and saved her.** Caderousse was, like Fernand, enrolled in army, but, being married and eight years older, merely sent to frontier. **Old Dantès, who was only sustained by hope, lost all hope at Napoleon's downfall. Five months after he had been separated from his son, and almost at hour of his arrest, he breathed his last in Mercédès' arms. M. Morrel paid expenses of his funeral, and few small debts poor old man had contracted.** Louis XVIII made but faint attempt to parry unexpected blow; monarchy tottered; at sign from emperor incongruous structure fell. Villefort gained nothing save king's gratitude (rather likely to injure him) and cross of Legion of Honor, which he had prudence not to wear. **Napoleon would have deprived Villefort of his office had it not been for Noirtier, who was all powerful at court; thus the Girondin of '93 and Senator of 1806 protected him who so lately had been his protector.** All Villefort's influence barely enabled him to stifle secret Dantès had so nearly divulged. Scarcely had emperor re-entered Tuileries when Marseilles began, despite authorities, to rekindle flames of civil war. Villefort retained his place, but his marriage was put off until more favorable opportunity. Worthy shipowner Morrel became sufficiently influential to make demand in favor of Dantès.

**Villefort and Morrel's confrontation (spring Year 10)**: Villefort was deputy procureur, first magistrate of Marseilles, when M. Morrel was announced. Villefort made Morrel wait in antechamber, although he had no one with him, for simple reason that king's procureur always makes everyone wait; after quarter hour reading papers, ordered Morrel admitted. **Morrel: "Monsieur, do you recollect that a few days before landing of his majesty the emperor, I came to intercede for young man, mate of my ship, who was accused of being concerned in correspondence with Island of Elba? What was other day a crime is today title to favor. You then served Louis XVIII, and you did not show any favor—it was your duty; today you serve Napoleon, and you ought to protect him—it is equally your duty; I come, therefore, to ask what has become of him?"** Villefort gazed at Morrel as if had difficulty recognizing him; honest shipowner turned his hat in his hands. **Had Morrel been more quick-sighted or better versed in such matters, he would have been surprised at king's procureur answering him on such subject, instead of referring him to governors of prison or prefect of department.** Villefort said: **"It has always been so, my dear Morrel, since reign of Louis XIV. The emperor is more strict in prison discipline than even Louis himself, and number of prisoners whose names are not on register is incalculable."** **Villefort dictated petition, in which, from excellent intention, Dantès' patriotic services were exaggerated, and he was made out one of most active agents of Napoleon's return. It was evident that at sight of this document minister would instantly release him.** **Instead of sending to Paris, Villefort carefully preserved petition that so fearfully compromised Dantès, in hopes of event that seemed not unlikely—second restoration. Dantès remained prisoner, and heard not noise of fall of Louis XVIII's throne, or still more tragic destruction of empire.** **Danglars comprehended full extent of wretched fate overwhelming Dantès; when Napoleon returned to France, he termed coincidence "decree of Providence."** **When Napoleon returned to Paris, Danglars' heart failed him; he lived in constant fear of Dantès' return on mission of vengeance. He therefore informed M. Morrel of wish to quit sea, obtained recommendation to Spanish merchant, into whose service he entered at end of March (ten or twelve days after Napoleon's return). He then left for Madrid, was no more heard of.**

**Prison inspection and Dantès' plea (after Louis XVIII's 1815 restoration)**: A year after Louis XVIII's restoration, inspector-general of prisons visited. Dantès in his cell heard noise of preparation—sounds that at his depth would have been inaudible to any but ear of prisoner, who could hear splash of drop of water that every hour fell from roof of his dungeon. He guessed something uncommon was passing among living; but he had so long ceased to have any intercourse with world, that he looked upon himself as dead. Inspector visited cells and dungeons of several prisoners whose good behavior or stupidity recommended them to clemency of government. He inquired how they were fed, and if they had any request to make. Universal response was that fare was detestable, and that they wanted to be set free. Governor told inspector of old abbé in dungeon about twenty feet distant, formerly leader of party in Italy, imprisoned since 1811, went mad in 1813; change is astonishing—used to weep, now laughs; grew thin, now grows fat. Inspector agreed to see him. At sound of key turning in lock and creaking of hinges, Dantès, crouched in corner of dungeon, whence he could see ray of light through narrow iron grating above, raised his head. Seeing stranger escorted by two turnkeys holding torches and accompanied by two soldiers, and to whom governor spoke bareheaded, Dantès guessed truth—moment to address himself to superior authorities had come—sprang forward with clasped hands. Soldiers interposed their bayonets, for they thought he was about to attack inspector, and inspector recoiled two or three steps. Dantès saw he was looked upon as dangerous. Then, infusing all humility he possessed into his eyes and voice, addressed inspector and sought to inspire him with pity. Inspector listened attentively; turning to governor, observed: "He will become religious—he is already more gentle; he is afraid, and retreated before bayonets—madmen are not afraid of anything; I made some curious observations on this at Charenton." Then, turning to prisoner: "What is it you want?" Dantès replied: "Only seventeen months... Oh, you do not know what is seventeen months in prison!—seventeen ages rather, especially to man who, like me, had arrived at summit of his ambition—to man, like me, was on point of marrying woman he adored, who saw honorable career opened before him, and who loses all in instant—who sees his prospects destroyed, and is ignorant of fate of his affianced wife, and whether his aged father be still living! Seventeen months' captivity to sailor accustomed to boundless ocean, is worse punishment than human crime ever merited. Have pity on me then, and ask for me, not intelligence, but trial; not pardon, but verdict—trial, sir, I ask only for trial; that, surely, cannot be denied to one who is accused!" **Government policy against allowing victims of persecution to reappear: despotic governments fear ear that hears their orders and eye that scrutinizes their actions. Madness always concealed in cell, from whence, should it depart, conveyed to some gloomy hospital, where doctor has no thought for man or mind in mutilated being jailer delivers to him. The very madness of Abbé Faria, gone mad in prison, condemned him to perpetual captivity.**

## Marius and Cosette: Courtship to Death Vigil

**Spring Year 6 confessions through barricade**: Marius revealed orphan status, lawyer profession, father colonel-hero. Cosette revealed convent upbringing, dead mother, father M. Fauchelevent. Éponine died leading Marius to barricade. Witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed. Shot broke collar bone. Vigorous hand seized him before consciousness vanished.

**Medical recovery and wedding (1 February 1833)**: Doctor declared recovery assured. Learned Cosette was not daughter of old man she called father; another Fauchelevent was real father. Dowry: five hundred eighty thousand francs, constituted legacy by dead person desiring to remain unknown. **Wedding at church of Saint-Paul: Cosette wore white taffeta petticoat, Binche guipure robe, English point veil, pearl necklace, orange flower wreath. Route: Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. Jean Valjean rose, left unperceived during celebration.**

**Javert's death and estrangement**: Javert drowned in Seine. **RUMOR—Marius suspects Jean Valjean killed Javert in barricade.**

**Jean Valjean's revelation and withdrawal**: **Proclaimed: "I am an ex-convict."** Marius shocked, concluded Jean Valjean horrible workman but admirable work. Address changed to _you_, "Madame," "Monsieur Jean." Cosette became more gay, less tender. One day chanced to say "father." "Say Jean"—She replied: "Ah! truly, Monsieur Jean." Complete extinction ensued. Neatly clad in black, emerged daily at same hour towards nightfall from Rue de l'Homme Armé. **He was eighty years old; before Marius' marriage, would have hardly been taken for fifty; that year had counted for thirty.** Later confined to apartment, then bed. **Revealed black jet from England, white jet from Norway; invented way of substituting slides; six hundred thousand francs made. Also managed very well with glass goods. Adjured Marius: "Have no fear, the six hundred thousand francs really belong to Cosette!"** **[Heard by God alone]: "All is over. I shall never see her more... What is frightful is to die without seeing her."** Final decline: breath intermittent; difficulty moving forearm; feet lost all movement. As wretchedness of limb increased, all majesty of soul displayed. Light of unknown world visible in eyes. **In cemetery of Père-Lachaise, vicinity of common grave, far from elegant quarter, in deserted corner beside old wall, beneath great yew tree over which climbs wild convolvulus, amid dandelions and mosses, lies stone.**

## Thénardier's Blackmail and Marius's Confrontation

**Thénardier's discovery and exposure**: Through daughter Azelma tracking married pair, discovered Cosette was Madame la Baronne Pontmercy. **Offered to drive individual from family who has no right there; claimed twenty thousand francs as price.** **Wore black cloth coat, silk waistcoat, boots, green glasses, plastered gray hair. With agility of monkey, tore off spectacles, withdrew two quills from nose, took off face as man takes off hat.**

**Marius's confrontation and evidence**: Revealed Javert's suicide facts announced in _Moniteur_ 15th June, 1832: Javert reported to prefect that, having been taken prisoner in barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie, he owed his life to magnanimity of insurgent who, holding him under pistol, fired into air instead of blowing out his brains. **Marius possessed evidence, certain date, irrefragable proof. "You are an infamous wretch! you are a liar, a calumniator, a villain... you have only succeeded in glorifying him. And it is you who are the thief! And it is you who are the assassin! I saw you, Thénardier Jondrette, in that lair on the Rue de l'Hôpital."** Offered twenty thousand francs total, ordered him to America with daughter; wife dead. **The moral wretchedness of Thénardier was irremediable. He was in America what he had been in Europe. With Marius' money, Thénardier set up as slave-dealer.**
